studies.title: Nearer Than The Vein
studies.meaning: A rhetorical question opens the passage: did the first making tire Us. The answer is not given, because the question is the answer, and the doubt named is about a second making. Then the argument turns inward. The whispering a person barely admits to himself is already known, and nearness is measured against a vein inside his own neck. Scholars differ over whether the nearness is God's knowledge or His angels, and both readings are recorded.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, from a surah that argues almost entirely with people who found resurrection absurd. The ayat just before list earlier communities that rejected their messengers, so the passage sits between a historical list and a scene of death. No specific occasion is reported. The audience were people who buried their dead in dry ground and had watched bodies become indistinguishable from the earth around them.

keyTerms.note: An onomatopoeic verb imitating a faint continuous sound, used of jewellery rustling. It names the half-formed traffic of the mind rather than decided thought, which is the level the ayah claims is known.
Literally the cord of the neck vessel. The comparison is not to something far away made close but to the nearest thing a person has, inside the skin, which he still cannot see or feel.
A dual participle from a verb meaning to meet and take from. They are described as receiving rather than watching, so the record is presented as something handed over rather than something caught.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Privacy in a Meccan house was thin. Families slept in one room, courtyards were shared, and a man's business was conducted in the open at the edge of the market. The one place nobody could reach was the inside of your own head, and that was where a person kept the thing he could not say. Arabia also knew the jugular precisely, from slaughtering animals, where the cut is made at that vein.
studies.didYouKnow: Surah 50 is one of only three that open with a single disconnected letter. A companion is reported to have said she learned this surah by heart only from hearing the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) recite it from the pulpit on Fridays, which means the congregation heard it something like fifty times a year.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Nearness and knowledge are joined here in a way that resists a common picture of God as distant and watching from above. The vein is inside the body, so the passage places God closer to a person than that person's own attention reaches. It also settles the resurrection argument by scale: an act already performed once cannot be too hard the second time, and the doubt is relocated from God's capacity to the doubter's imagination.

crossReferences.why: States the same nearness as an answer to a question about where God is, and ties it to calling on Him.
Answers the opening question directly, saying the repetition of creation is the easier of the two acts.
Describes the same recording pair from a different angle, naming them honourable and saying they know what is done.

studies.applyIt: Tonight, before you sleep, sit for two minutes and let your mind run without steering it. Do not pray, do not plan, do not correct anything. Just watch what comes up first. This passage says that layer is already known, so the exercise is not disclosure. It is getting acquainted with material that is being recorded whether or not you look at it.

studies.title: And With Us Is More
studies.meaning: Two lines of paradise and then a hard turn. The greeting on entry is peace and the day is named for its permanence, which answers the anxiety that everything good ends. Then a phrase the commentators dwell on: whatever they wish, and with Us is more, an unspecified surplus beyond desire itself. The passage then swings to destroyed civilisations and closes by naming who can hear any of it, a person with a heart or an ear genuinely present.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in a surah built as a single sustained argument about the Hour. No specific occasion is reported. The generations mentioned were not abstractions to the first audience: the ruins of earlier Arabian peoples lay along the trade roads north, and Meccan caravans passed abandoned settlements every season. The rhetorical question about escape is addressed to people who had seen what was left of those who tried.

keyTerms.note: An indefinite noun with no object attached, so the sentence deliberately does not say more of what. Classical readers gathered many suggestions and generally left the word open, which is what its grammar does.
From a root meaning to remain without change or decay, used in Arabic of long-lived things generally. Naming the day itself by that word puts the permanence in the day rather than only in the people.
The idiom is throwing your hearing at something, an act of aim rather than reception. It is paired with being present, so listening while elsewhere in mind is excluded by the phrasing.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The road from Mecca to Syria ran past the dwellings of peoples the Quran names, cut into rock and long empty. Traders camped near them. Arabian memory kept these places as warnings rather than as history, recited in poetry and pointed out to children on the journey. A merchant who made the northern run twice a year passed more ruined cities than living ones, and knew exactly how much force had not saved them.
studies.didYouKnow: The single word rendered as more at the end of the second ayah drew a long tradition of comment, and one report preserved in the early collections explains it as the sight of God, granted after every desire has already been met. The Quran leaves it unspecified. The grammar does the work: an increase with no stated limit.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage ends by naming the condition for hearing, and the condition is not intelligence or information. A heart, or an ear lent while actually present. That places the difference between the two audiences of this surah inside the listener rather than in the evidence, since both groups have the same ruins on the same road. The surplus promised beyond every desire also implies that human wanting is not the ceiling of what can be given.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same open-ended promise of an increase beyond the best reward, without naming what the increase is.
Repeats the argument from ruined civilisations, granting that they were stronger and asking what it saved.
Names the opposite of the listener described here, hearing that is present in body and absent in use.

studies.applyIt: Listen to one thing today with your whole attention: a recitation, a friend's account of their week, a lecture you would normally half-hear. Put the phone in another room. Fifteen minutes is enough. The last ayah makes presence the qualification, and presence is a physical arrangement before it is a spiritual one.
